Speculative decoding is a technique designed to increase throughput by letting a smaller "draft" model propose multiple tokens before the larger "target" model verifies them. Instead of generating one token at a time through the heavy model, you generate $k$ candidates quickly and check them all in a single forward pass.

The key insight is that this isn't an approximation; the method uses a modified rejection-sampling rule so that the final output distribution remains exactly the same as if the target model had generated everything alone. However, the speedup isn't infinite. Accepted tokens grow sublinearly with the number of drafts because every new token requires all previous ones to be accepted. Once the draft model becomes too large or complex, the cost of running it offsets the savings from skipping target inference steps.

According to Leviathan et al. (ICML 2023), past a certain point, additional speculation is paid for and discarded, making the optimal draft length usually quite small.

As noted in the reference material, these absolute rotations cancel out during the attention score calculation, meaning only the difference in position remains.

In contrast, fixed embeddings often break when extrapolating beyond their maximum training length because they rely on specific positional values that don't exist yet.
